title: Tuning a model: settings and search
hook: Defaults, manual tweaks, grid, random and smarter search, and when to stop.
inPlainWords: Most models have settings you choose before training, like how deep a tree may grow. Tuning means trying settings and keeping the best, judged on data the model did not learn from. The biggest gains usually come from better data and features, not from endless tuning.

useCase.title: Squeeze more accuracy from the cancellation model
useCase.story: The boosted-tree cancellation model scores 86% on the exam set. The team has three weeks and a modest computer budget. Settings include how many trees, how deep they grow, and how fast it learns. Should they keep tuning, and how?

approaches.name: Start with the defaults
approaches.what: Use the library's sensible starting settings.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never skip it. It may already be enough.

approaches.name: Manual tweaks
approaches.what: Change one setting by hand and re-check.
approaches.greatWhen: You want to learn how the model reacts.
approaches.avoidWhen: Many settings interact and you get lost.

approaches.name: Grid search
approaches.what: Try every combination from a fixed list.
approaches.example: 3 depths by 3 speeds by 3 tree counts is 27 runs.

approaches.name: Random search
approaches.what: Try random combinations within sensible ranges.
approaches.greatWhen: Many settings. It usually finds good areas faster than a grid.

approaches.name: Smarter search
approaches.what: Use earlier results to choose the next try.
approaches.avoidWhen: Runs are cheap, and random search is enough.
approaches.example: A tool proposes new settings based on past runs.

approaches.name: Automated tuning (AutoML)
approaches.what: A tool tunes and compares models for you.
approaches.avoidWhen: You must understand and control every step.
approaches.example: Upload the table and let it search.

approaches.name: Improve the data and features instead
approaches.what: Better inputs instead of better settings.

challenge.question: The model scores 86% and there are three weeks left. What is the smartest use of the time?

options.text: Improve features first, then run a random or smarter search with a time limit, judged on a validation slice and tested once on the final exam
options.why: Data first, then a bounded search, with an honest final score.

options.text: Run a giant grid search over every setting
options.why: The cost explodes and gains are small.

options.text: Tune until the exam score is perfect, reusing the same exam every time
options.why: The search memorizes the exam, so the score is fake.

options.text: Stop and ship with no comparison
options.why: Cheap, but you never learn if it could be better.

bestCase.title: Data first, a bounded search, and one honest final test
bestCase.example: New features lift the score from 85% to 87%. A one-day random search of 40 tries, judged on a validation slice, finds settings worth another point. A single final test on the untouched exam gives 88%, which holds up live.

worstCase.title: Tuning against the final exam
worstCase.example: Every try is scored on the same exam set. After 500 tries the exam score is 93%, but the search has learned the exam's quirks. Live accuracy is 84%, and the team cannot work out why.

route.travelling: Cancellation model, 86% on the exam set

steps.label: Score tries on validation data
steps.goes: Each try is judged on a slice kept apart from the final exam.
steps.goesWrong: Every try is judged on the final exam, so the search memorizes the exam.

steps.label: Test once on the final exam
Record the settings
steps.goes: Save them with the model version.

takeaway: Fix the data first, then search settings with a budget, and keep the final exam untouched until the end.
